title: Correlation between welding structure and corrosion behavior of high strength low alloy (HSLA) ship steel in Cl--containing solutions
abstract: The high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel industry is in great demand due to the continued growth of the ship and marine sectors. The microstructure of HSLA steel is greatly influenced by both the heat input during welding and the variations in salinity resulting from changes in climate. This paper presents the development of HSLA ship steel using a vacuum electric arc furnace and heat treatment techniques. Electrochemical corrosion tests were conducted on the substrate, heat-affected zone, and fused zone of HSLA ship steel. The results showed that the heat treatment process can improve the microstructure homogeneity of the HSLA ship steel, eliminate chemical composition segregation, refine the grain, and promote the formation of the microstructure of pearlite and ferrite. The welded interface structure was uniform and free from defects or inclusions. The metallographic microstructure of the fused zone showed a massive distribution of grain boundary ferrite, martensite, and granular bainite, and that of the heat-affected zone displayed superheated characteristics consisting of pearlite and acicular ferrite. The interlocking microstructure of the base material enhanced performance in a 4.2 % NaCl solution. The corrosion resistance of the heat-affected zone and fused zones of HSLA ship steel deteriorated. Grain boundary ferrite may be related to the inferior corrosion resistance of the heat-affected zone, while the coarse microstructure of granular bainite led to the serious corrosion resistance in the fused zone of HSLA ship steel.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The application of high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel has seen a significant increase due to the growing complexity of its usage, highlighting the necessity for the development of novel HSLA steel  [1] . The key performance indicator for HSLA steel is to provide sufficient impact toughness at low temperatures (− 20 °C), along with strong yield strength and tensile strength  [2] . HSLA steel is low-carbon steel with a carbon content below 0.45 %, and it exhibits excellent weldability and yield strength exceeding 520 MPa  [3] . The composition usually consists of Ni, Cr, Mo, and other alloying elements. A fine-grain structure is present in the as-cast state  [4,5] . The extensive development of global marine resources in recent years has led to a significant deterioration in the environment for ship service. As a result, there is a need to develop HSLA ship steel with environmental adaptability  [6] .

Heat treatment techniques such as normalizing or quenching followed by tempering are commonly used for HSLA steel. Both techniques rely on a similar mechanism that involves a rapid cooling rate to reduce or eliminate internal stresses and achieve optimal properties  [7] . In general, HSLA steel is normalized to obtain bainitic ferrite and subsequently tempered at 500–650 °C to maintain traces of sorbite and ferrite, resulting in enhanced mechanical properties  [8] . The tensile strength after welding can reach 520.8 MPa, and the impact energy can reach 122.1 J through the use of normalizing and tempering processes, meeting the minimum service environment requirements  [9] . Controlling the brittleness through tempering is also crucial. Anastasiia  [10]  conducted a systematic study on the effects of tempering temperature (600 °C, 650 °C, 700 °C) on the microstructure and properties of HSLA steel and achieved an outstanding resultant strength of 690 MPa after tempering at 700 °C. Therefore, the key to improving the toughness performance of HSLA ship steel is the selection of appropriate heat treatment processes.

In the manufacturing process of shipbuilding with HSLA steels, welding is undoubtedly an essential process  [1,11] . Studies reveal that vulnerabilities in welded joints are of utmost importance for ensuring the safe operation of ships  [12] , particularly in the fused zone  [13,14] , which experiences the recurrent accumulation of heat from unimodal and multimodal sequences, resulting in a relatively inhomogeneous microstructure  [15] . The quality of welded joints cannot be inaccessible due to factors including heat input  [16]  and the base material preheating  [17] , which exert a significant impact on the fatigue properties and corrosion resistance of the welded bead  [12,18]  in HSLA steel. Along this path, the focus of this research is on optimizing existing welding processes and selecting appropriate heat treatment procedures for HSLA ship steel to enhance its performance.

The corrosion resistance of HSLA ship steel faces numerous challenges when exposed to varying seawater concentrations. The global ocean fluctuates between 3.1 % and 3.8 % Cl -  concentration due to the different effects of evaporation, sedimentation, and dilution caused by water circulation  [19] . Different concentrations of Cl -  can affect the corrosion behavior of the base material, heat-affected zone, and weld bead, resulting in significant differences  [20] . The complex corrosion behavior of welded joints often leads to the weak link of the ship’s structure when exposed to discrepancy concentration  [22] . Nevertheless, variations in metallurgical effects, geometry, and specific environmental conditions can result in different forms of corrosion, including galvanic corrosion, pitting, and stress corrosion cracking (SCC)  [21] . To date, there have not been many studies on the impact of HSLA ship steel microstructure on corrosion behavior after welding under varying Cl -  concentrations. Therefore, relevant research in this area is urgently needed.

The novel HSLA ship steel is prepared using an electric arc furnace and heat treatment process, and its microstructure characteristics and interface are verified using material morphology analysis methods. Welding and electrochemical corrosion tests are conducted. The electrochemical corrosion performance and corrosion morphology of base materials, heat-affected zones, and fused zones of HSLA ship steel were analyzed.

sections.heading: Preparation of HSLA ship steel
paragraphs:
The experiment utilized a range of raw materials, including industrial pure iron, high-quality scraps, carbon enhancers, ferrosilicon, deoxidizers, nickel, ferromanganese, ferrochrome, ferromolybdenum, and ferrovanadium. The steel was made using a mix of high-quality and ordinary scrap in an 8:2 ratio, along with industrial pure iron used to regulate the carbon concentration.  
                         Table 1  displays the composition of the HSLA steel. Adding a moderate amount of Ni, Cr, and V improves the workability and weldability of the HSLA steel  [23] , helps to avoid the sensitization mechanism caused by Cr-rich carbides, and achieves improved oxidation resistance. The chosen method for melting the steel was the electric arc furnace. Along with inserting aluminum wire at a ratio of lime to fluorite of 5:1. A sample measuring 150 mm × 150 mm × 500 mm was poured to examine the impact of casting size on internal defects and the heat treatment process.

sections.heading: Heat treatment of HSLA ship steel
paragraphs:
The heat treatment process included normalizing, quenching, tempering, and diffusion annealing. The specific heat treatment process curve is shown in  
                         Fig. 1 . The final samples were cut into pieces measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 15 mm. Subsequently, it was polished, ground, and etched for observation and analysis with a metallographic microscope.

As  
                         Fig. 2 (a) illustrates, the as-cast microstructure exhibits localized grain coarsening and comprises a ferrite and pearlite combination. The ferrite exhibited predominantly acicular and block-like morphologies, while the pearlite was identifiable as the darker region. Following normalization and tempering heat treatment processes, the metallographic photograph of the sample is presented in  Fig. 2 (b). Upon reaching the tempering state, the specimens revealed a microstructure of tempered sorbite with a minor austenite presence, the microstructure itself being finer and more uniformly distributed.

The mechanical properties of the test specimens, post-two tempering treatments, and their as-cast condition are evaluated, and their results are shown in  
                         Table 2 . The observed absence of the lower yield strength in the as-cast specimen was due to the grain coarsening. The treated sample demonstrated substantial improvements over the as-cast sample, with yield strength measured at 555.8 MPa and a marked enhancement in impact energy.

sections.heading: Welding process of HSLA ship steel
paragraphs: The welding experiment was conducted according to Chinese standard GB/T 17493-2008. The E7515-G electrode wire was used, and a welding current of 80 A was selected for the electrode arc welding. Before welding, the HSLA ship steel specimens were annealed and preheated at 125–200 °C, which may reduce heat buildup issues and alleviate residual stresses  [24] . The interface specimen was processed into metallographic specimens and examined under a metallographic microscope.

sections.heading: Electrochemical corrosion of HSLA ship steel
paragraphs:
The corrosion resistance of HSLA ship steel in the fused zone, heat-affected zone, and base material, referred to as FZ, HAZ, and BM, at different NaCl concentrations (3.0 wt%, 3.4 wt%, 3.8 wt%, and 4.2 wt%) was investigated using an Interface 1010E electrochemical workstation. Before electrochemical testing, samples from selected discrepancy locations (the sampling schematic is shown in  
                         Fig. 3 ) were processed by being cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm and then degreased by immersing in acetone and using ultrasonication. The non-working side of the specimen is sealed in the tube with resin, leaving the working side smoothed on the test surface, polished, cleaned, and dried using a desiccator. The potentiodynamic polarization curve and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were employed to analyze the corrosion resistance of a three-electrode system (a platinum counter electrode, a saturated calomel reference electrode (SCE), and a working electrode). Constant potential polarization was first performed for 90 s with a − 1.0 V cathodic potential. Then, the specimens were tested for open-circuit potential (OCP) in solution for at least 1 h. When the OCP was stabilized, the EIS was tested with a frequency set from 10 −2  Hz to 10 4  Hz and a sine wave amplitude of 10 mV, as indicated by previous work  [24] . The potentiodynamic polarization curves were measured at a scan rate of 0.17 mV/s and a scan range of − 0.5 V to 0.5 V (vs. OCP). The corrosion samples were then observed and analyzed using optical microscopy (OM) and the S-3400N scanning electron microscope (SEM). A VW-9000 high-speed microscope (HSM) in 3D profiles was used to observe the geometry of the corrosion product.

sections.heading: Electrochemical corrosion behavior of HSLA ship steel
paragraphs: Fig. 4  displays the potentiodynamic polarization curves and EIS plots of BM in solutions of NaCl with concentrations of 3.0 wt%, 3.4 wt%, 3.8 wt%, and 4.2 wt%, respectively. The corrosion potential (E corr ) is one of the primary factors influencing the behavior of materials when exposed to various corrosive media. E corr  can be used to determine the tendency of a material to undergo self-corrosion and its susceptibility to a stronger corrosion tendency in corrosive media. As shown in  Fig. 4 (a), the polarization curves of BM exhibit a positive shift at high concentrations, shifting from − 0.437 V to − 0.684 V, − 0.502 V, and − 0.389 V, respectively. This result illustrated that BM exhibited the most severe tendency to corrode in the 3.4 wt% NaCl solution. Furthermore, the anodic curve of BM did not vary significantly within all concentration ranges, demonstrating the behavior of metal activation and the similarity in the principle of anodic and cathodic reactions, indicating a combination of oxygen reduction and hydrogen evolution reactions in the cathodic region and an active dissolution process in the anodic region, devoid of 3.4 %. Tafel analysis is used to fit the polarization curves and obtain the corrosion current density (I corr ) of HSLA ship steel at different concentration levels. The order of I corr  values at different concentrations of NaCl of 3.0 wt%, 3.4 wt%, 3.8 wt%, and 4.2 wt% was 2.0228 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , 5.388 × 10 −6  A/cm 2 , 4.3547 × 10 −6  A/cm 2 , 1.982 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , respectively. This indicated that BM has the fastest corrosion rate in a NaCl solution with a concentration of 3.0 wt%. Generally, Cl -  can accelerate the anodic dissolution due to their small radii, allowing them to penetrate the corrosion scale and alter the interface environment. However, Cl -  can have the opposite effect on anodic dissolution for two main reasons. First, the formation of corrosion products reduces the number of active sites on the metal surface. Second, Cl -  can act as an inhibitor of hydrogen absorption, decreasing the electrochemical reaction rate at high NaCl concentrations. Therefore, the state of the corrosion product can significantly impact the rate of anodic dissolution. Enhanced insight into this complex situation can be obtained through EIS measurements.

Fig. 4 (b) shows the EIS plots of the HSLA ship steel BM at different concentrations of NaCl solutions. In the Nyquist plots, the larger the capacitive semicircle radius, the better the corrosion resistance. The size of the capacitive semicircle radius was in the order of 3.0 wt%, 3.4 wt%, 3.8 wt%, and 4.2 wt%, following the level of corrosion resistance. The BM showed an elongated semicircular arc, which could be explained by a non-uniform surface charge transfer mechanism. Furthermore, oxygen diffusion was dominant.

The number of peaks in the Bode plot can determine the time constant generated by the corrosion process.  Fig. 4 (c) indicates that the time constant was the same regardless of the concentration of NaCl solutions, illustrating a correlation between the corrosion process and charge transfer resistance. An increase in phase angle with frequency signified the presence of corrosion products. In the presence of high NaCl concentrations, minor variation was evident in both low- and high-frequency phase angles. The low-frequency phase consistently maintained a high level, correlating with the low-frequency peaks of the corrosion process. The data indicates that the peak Z modulus and phase angle values at low frequencies suggested a diminished corrosion process in solution with high NaCl concentrations, supporting the findings from the Nyquist plots. In the case of BM, the mid-frequency peak potentially governs the formation and growth of the corrosion products  [24] . The peak increased with the concentration, as it signified the build-up of corrosion products and a reduction in metal dissolution, leading to an increase in the impedance data. In essence, the dissolution of the exposes specimen, resulting in the release of Fe 2+ , is facilitated, resulting in the formation of relatively stable corrosion products at high NaCl concentrations. The presence of secondary precipitated phases can exert a dominant impact on the corrosion properties under specific heat treatment conditions  [7] . Based on the actual magnitude of the Bode phase plot, the corrosion state was worse at 3.0 wt%, meaning a lower NaCl concentration state was worse at 3.0 wt%, corroborating the finding from the potentiodynamic polarization curves and the Nyquist plots. This further confirmed the improved EIS behavior of the BM at higher concentrations of NaCl solution compared to the lower ones.

sections.heading: The microstructure of HSLA ship steel after welding
paragraphs: Fig. 5 (a) shows the metallographic microstructure of HAZ, with a predominant distribution of grain boundary ferrite, acicular ferrite, and pearlite precipitated along ferrite, which is consistent with the previous work  [13,25] . The acicular ferrite is a commonly substructured, non-equiaxial phase produced during the continuous cooling process at a temperature range slightly higher than that of upper bainite.  Fig. 5 (b) shows the metallographic microstructure of the welding interface, which demonstrates a uniform, fine interface bond state with no defects or inclusions. This interface consists of a strip and an acicular distribution of ferrite and the first eutectic ferrite. Along the columnar grain boundary, fine, denser acicular ferrite grow inward with a small amount of pearlite microstructure and a certain amount of granular bainite immediately adjacent to the first eutectic ferrite. In the middle and at the top of FZ, the lower temperature gradient allowed for the growth of specimens and the formation of a coarser columnar microstructure after exposure to high temperatures. The microstructure of the FZ consists of granular bainite with the prior austenite grain interiors and a small amount of Widmanstӓtten ferrite growing off the prior austenite grain boundaries  [11,14] , as shown in  Fig. 5 (c).  Fig. 5 (d) indicates a relatively lower dilution between the HSLA ship steel and E7515-G.

The changes in the microstructure of the HAZ were due to the heating process during the welding. The first austenite grains nucleates and sprouted along with austenitization to produce a phenomenon of local concentration of carbon and alloying elements, resulting in a phenomenon of local concentration of carbon and alloying elements and the transformation of austenite into acicular ferrite. The microstructure is not coarsened, hindering the precipitation of ferrite and inducing the conversion of the second phase, consisting of Widmanstӓtten ferrite and upper bainite. Coarse superheated austenite formed from cooling are not conducive to improving the high-angle grain boundaries but instead promoted crack expansion. This has a negative influence on corrosion resistance  [25] . Additionally, the microstructure along with cooling can indicate the presence of carbon-depleted zones in the HAZ, which result from carbon migration  [26] . Near the interface, as shown in  Fig. 5 (b), there was no obvious indication of a carbon-depleted zone. The microstructure of the superheated zone determines the brittleness zone, which is prone to cracking and represents the weak link in the welded joint  [27] . When compared to  Fig. 5 (c) and  Fig. 2 , it could be observed that the microstructure distribution of BM is more uniform than in the FZ, and its grain is denser. The microstructure of FZ was propinquity, but the shape of ferrite in the HAZ is acicular and grain boundary-size. According to Patterson’s work  [28] , the existence of grain boundary ferrite in the HAZ is possible due to carbide precipitation increasing the number of nucleation sites for the formation of grain boundary ferrites. Furthermore, the existence of grain boundary ferrite decreases the fractions of bainite and Widmanstӓtten ferrite. Conversely, the distribution of prior austenite grain boundaries was net-like due to preferential nucleation sites in FZ.

sections.heading: Electrochemical corrosion behavior of welded joints
paragraphs:
The potentiodynamic polarization curves and EIS plots are obtained for the HAZ in NaCl solutions with concentrations of 3.0 wt%, 3.4 wt%, 3.8 wt%, and 4.2 wt% are shown in  
                         Fig. 6 . As demonstrated in  Fig. 6 (a), the regions of anodic and cathodic are asymmetrical. Based on the shape of potentiodynamic polarization curves, the anodic reaction was dominated by the active dissolution of iron, while the cathodic reaction was synergistically controlled by oxygen reduction and hydrogen evolution.  
                         Table 3  lists the corresponding fitting data. The E corr  of HAZ at different concentrations was − 0.513 V, − 0.913 V, − 0.639 V, and − 0.919 V, respectively. The lowest E corr  occurred at 4.2 wt% NaCl solution, revealing that the HAZ exhibits greater susceptibility to corrosion. The I corr  of HAZ at different concentrations was 2.2574 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , 2.3242 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , 2.6345 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , and 2.9582 × 10 −5  A/cm 2 , respectively. The corrosion rate of the HAZ reached a maximum at concentrations of 4.2 wt% NaCl solution. The appearance of the wield pattern can be attributed to the complexity of different features in HAZ. Different microstructures form many types of microstructures when exposed to a discrepancy in NaCl concentration solution, making the irregularity of the polarization curve occur  [13] .

In addition, the Nyquist plots in  Fig. 6 (b) do not display perfect semicircles due to the dispersion of interfacial impedance with frequency. The size of the capacitive semicircle radius increased in sequence as follows: 4.2 wt%, 3.8 wt%, 3.4 wt%, and 3.0 wt%. The highest impedance of the HAZ in a 3.0 wt% NaCl solution suggested better resistance to charge transfer.

The Bode plots of HAZ at different concentrations are depicted in  Fig. 6 (c). The impedance spectrum remained similar to that of the BM, with only one time constant present at any concentration. The low and high-frequency phase angles were nearly equal, particularly in the low-frequency region approaching 0°, even reaching 0° at 4.2 wt% concentration, suggesting a lack of correlation between concentrations and corrosion product behavior and the appearance of the less significant variation in the corrosion mechanism, which consisted of the shape of potentiodynamic polarization curves. However, the only difference was the peak angle, with the concentration of peak values ranging from 70° to 63°, 61°, and 56°, illustrating the HAZ showing the appearance of corrosion products at all concentrations. The modal magnitude of the HAZ samples decreased as the NaCl concentration increased. This indicated that the reduced resistance of the metal oxidation process led to a deterioration in the corrosion resistance of the surface with increasing concentrations of NaCl solution. Additionally, the coupling resulting from factors such as microstructure and composition can either hasten or slow down the corrosion behavior of the microstructure and cause significant differences in grain size, impacting the stability of corrosion products in a corrosive environment. The level of galvanic corrosion depends on the concentration of OH - . The surface pH, in the absence of cations, is primarily determined by the diffusion-limited reduction of dissolved oxygen. In the presence of oxygen reduction control at the cathode, OH -  is enriched on the local surface of the metal during galvanic corrosion, resulting in a decrease in the Cl -  sites  [14] . The coupling can activate the corrosion process in the exposed region where the cathode is suppressed. To obey the law of charge conservation, the anodic dissolution process is promoted. However, the HAZ exhibited a similar rate of decline in the mid-frequency region of the modal diagram, suggesting that the validity of the protective corrosion product was limited at any concentration  [24] . The results of the Bode and Modal charts were consistent with the pattern of the Nyquist plot.

Fig. 7  displays the potentiodynamic polarization curves and Nyquist plots of FZ samples in NaCl solutions at various concentrations. The cathodic polarization curves were characterized by mixed control of hydrogen evolution and oxygen reduction in 3.0 wt% and 4.2 wt%, and the left was dominantly hydrogen evolution. In  Fig. 7 (a), it is demonstrated that the corrosion resistance of FZ exhibited more corrosion-resistant characteristics with the increase of NaCl concentration. The polarization curve parameters for FZ in NaCl solutions are listed in  
                         Table 4 . The E corr  values of FZ at differing concentrations were − 0.627 V, − 0.623 V, − 0.724 V, and − 0.806 V, respectively, suggesting a tendency to corrode with increasing NaCl concentrations. The I corr  values of FZ sequentially increased as the normal order concentrations increased. The I corr  reached its upper limit at 3.0 wt% NaCl solution, illustrating that FZ corroded most rapidly, showing similar behavior compared to the observation in BM.

By comparing the EIS plots in  Fig. 7 (b), the FZ has the largest capacitive arc in a 4.2 wt% NaCl solution, demonstrating that it processes greater resistance to charge transfer and improved corrosion resistance at high concentrations.  Fig. 7 (c) displays the Bode plots of FZ at various concentrations. The impedance exhibited remarkable similarities to those observed in BM, with both having the same number of time constants. The low-frequency phase angles were all similar, while the high-frequency phase angles demonstrated a significant magnitude relationship, with the lowest value occurring at 3.0 wt% NaCl solution, even though the peak phase angle was at a high level. The presence of the initial peaks can be explained by the formation of corrosive products at high NaCl concentrations at the initial stage of the corrosive test. Then, the stability of the corrosion product at mid-frequency can be attributed to the combined influence of the galvanic factors H +  and Cl -  
                         [21,24] . The complexity of the pattern of corrosive resistance and the lack of regularity in the E corr  were the consequences of mixture influence. However, this could also act as an explanation for the difference in pattern between HAZ and FZ, which is prone to the discrepancy in grain size. The Model plot indicated that with an increase in frequency, the impedance gradually appears to decrease, which is very similar to BM. But the value of EIS was lower than that of BM, indicating a significant difference in grain size and a large number of types of precipitation. The grain size, which could be a significant factor influencing the corrosion resistance in FZ. Another significant thing that needs to be mentioned is the interaction between the intrusive hydrogen atoms and the coarse PAGBs.

Due to the assessment of corrosion resistance, post-welding becomes an imperative task. To further elucidate, identifying vulnerability at specific concentrations should be accorded paramount importance. Based on the results of the corrosion test in three zones, it could be found that the corrosion resistance of the BM and FZ would become a weak point in the actual service process. Therefore, a 3.0 % NaCl concentration solution are used to further fit the equivalent circuits for three zones, as shown in  
                         Fig. 8 . It could be noticed that the Nyquist plots all consisted of semicircles. The semi-circle above the real axis is associated with a capacitive effect. Therefore, the equivalent circuit utilized in the previous work  [29]  is used as a one-time constant capacitor model. R s  represented the solution resistance, whereas R p  represented the charge transfer resistance associated with double-layer capacitance CPE and its corresponding data, as listed in  
                         Table 5 . However, it is necessary to supplement the reason why CPE was chosen to represent the double layer, which may originate from the heterogeneous nature of the metal surface in the solution. In this system, the polarization resistance was the sum of the R p  resistance. This circumstance occurs when the measured Nyquist diagram only has one capacitive loop. This illustrates that the layer has not yet achieved the level of compactness necessary to establish its impedance loop. As reported by Guo  [30] , the charge transfer resistance has a relationship with the microstructure. The transformation of the microstructure caused by welding is inextricably linked to the change in R p  in the microstructure  [31,32] . This is why the value of R p  in the FZ is lower than in the other two zones. Nonetheless, the corrosion product layer can alter the path of dissolved oxygen diffusion, inhibiting some anions from infiltrating the corrosion product into the steel matrix and hence decelerating the corrosion rate to some extent  [33] . However, the presence of FZ with a coarse microstructure could not be excluded as a factor contributing to the formation of a large corroded area in the three zones attributed to the deriving force of galvanic corrosion. Galvanic corrosion represents one of the main corrosion mechanisms in welds  [21] . Maintaining a low ferrite content in the FZ of HSLA accelerates galvanic corrosion. And the results of the EIS are contradictory to the former findings  [34] .

Fig. 9  illustrates the 3D corrosion morphology and height variations in different zones of HSLA ship steel after electrochemical tests in a 3.0 wt% NaCl solution. The 3D surface profile of  Fig. 9 (a) shows the BM is covered with locally accumulated corrosion products. Similarly,  Fig. 9 (b) shows that the HAZ also exhibits localized accumulation, albeit with a broader range and thinner thickness than the BM. This also explained why HAZ is highly resistant to corrosion in a 3.0 wt% NaCl solution, compared to other concentrations. The thickness and range of corrosion deposits, occupying three zones, appeared to vary with the assistance of higher heat input, resulting in poor corrosion resistance. Moreover, there is a considerable accumulation of corrosion products in the FZ ( Fig. 9 (c) and (d)). Invariably, the microstructure of the steel and its corrosion resistance cannot be separated.

As can be seen in  Fig. 2 , the microstructure of the BM is tempered sorbite, a mixture of acicular ferrite, pearlite, and cementite structures. The tempered sorbite can not be directly unrelated to the formation of localized accumulations causing galvanic coupling. This coupling arises from the interaction between precipitates and the matrix, leading to continuous dissolution under existing Cl -  circumstances  [35,36] . The localized microstructure of the various phases also resulted in different degrees of galvanic corrosion. Another cause of galvanic coupling is the cementite in pearlite, which is electrochemically more stable than ferrite  [37] . However, the galvanic effect between the cementite and ferrite promotes ferrite corrosion, leading to a higher corrosion rate. This was why the BM exhibits localized corrosion in a 3.0 wt% NaCl solution. Regarding the HAZ, as shown in  Fig. 5 (a), this type of localized accumulation is most likely attributed to the significant presence of grain boundary ferrite. This is due to the grain boundary ferrite, which belongs to low-potential areas, being preferentially attacked by localized corrosion  [38] . This also explains why localized preferential dissolution occurs in HAZ.

Although it has been stated that AF in Cl -  solution is highly tolerant to covering a dense corrosion product, the irregular distribution of numerous grains of grain boundary ferrite leads to the formation of localized pockets of corrosion products  [36] . However, the height of corrosion product accumulation in FZ was significantly higher in smaller areas, about 270 % and 603 % higher than in BM and HAZ, respectively. This can be attributed to the oxygen reduction causing localized OH -  absorption. The microstructure of the FZ under the temperature gradient, resulting in coarse superheated austenite, was not conducive to improving the high-angle grain boundaries. Instead, it promotes crack expansion and has a negative influence on corrosion resistance  [25] . Additionally, it is well known that grain boundary boundaries are mostly high-angle ones, typically 15° or more  [36,37] . Thus, the structure of the nonequilibrium phase of the grain boundary is overshadowed by the acicular ferrite or tempered sorbite  [22,34] , which has a negative influence when exposed to the corrosive solution. This explained why the FZ exhibits a flat-lying state when exposed to the corrosive environment, resulting in a lower value of R p  and a higher value of CPE-T.

Fig. 10  exhibits the corrosion morphology of welded samples in a 3.0 wt% NaCl solution. The corrosive products of the BM consist of a small number of dimples and deeper microcracks that are relatively uniform, as shown in  Fig. 10  (a2) and (a3). Locally large stripped areas of the BM indicated that local corrosion products were particularly loose, as seen in the red box in  Fig. 10  (a2). In comparison to  Fig. 10  (b1) and (b2), a distinct behavior is observed in an exclusive behavior that happened in HAZ and seemed to be exhibited, the preferential dissolution, with localized more and wider microvoids, dimples, secondary microcracks, and the absence in BM. The corrosion morphology of the FZ samples is shown in  Fig. 10  (c2) and (c3). When comparing the corrosion morphology of localized HAZ and FZ, interconnected microvoids and dimples (white-colored areas) could be observed, which acted as stress concentration zones. However, their extent and number were larger in FZ  [7] .

The corrosion behavior is significantly influenced by the structure and thickness of the corrosion byproduct  [24,25] . The corrosion products of BM are relatively stable and uniform, with no obvious secondary cracks appearing, as shown in  Fig. 10  (a3), indicating better corrosion resistance. Visible microcracks were observed in the BM, but no microcracks were found in HAZ or FZ, indicating that the uneven microstructure of the BM may be responsible for the presence of these deep cracks. Additionally, the high temperature in the FZ had a significant effect on the microstructure of the heat-affected zone. Although the corrosion morphology of the HAZ reveals visible, consistent corrosion products ( Fig. 9 (b)), local secondary cracks and a small number of microvoids appeared, indicating the failure behavior of localized corrosion products. However, the occurrence of localized bigger microvoids ( Fig. 9  (b3)) in HAZ can be attributed to thermal stress, which residual stress failed to completely alleviate  [7] . However, in the case of the FZ, the corrosion morphology exhibits characteristics of anodic dissolution along the prior austenite grain boundaries at the bottom of pits, attributed to the high electrochemical activity and local acidification caused by Cl -  
                         [35] . Another reason explaining the difference in corrosion resistance between BM and FZ is the presence of different microstructures, as shown in  Fig. 9 (a) and (c). Moreover, the high-temperature gradient not only caused a coarse grain boundary but also led to the occurrence of segregation. This segregation affects the corrosion nucleation process, resulting in a relatively low level of corrosion resistance in the FZ  [39] . Nevertheless, the presence of cross-scale micropores is a key factor in the growth of corrosion products  [30,40] . This meant at a rate limited by the formation of corrosion products. The density of the corrosion product and its ability to inhibit Cl -  transmission are the keys to its protective properties  [33] . On the surfaces of FZ and HAZ, there were a certain number of relatively small porous and secondary microcracks, indicating that the corrosion products were relatively unstable. The presence of microvoids on the surface of the FZ was greater than on the HAZ, indicating that the microvoids started earlier in the FZ. Therefore, the presence of porous, corrosive, and toxic products covering the surfaces had an undeniable role in facilitating the penetration of experimental solutions into the matrix, thereby accelerating localized corrosion.

In recent years, significant changes have occurred in the salinity of the upper 400 m layer of the tropical Pacific Ocean, especially in the surface layer of the northern subtropical circulation area. The salinity trend was particularly notable in two places: the South Pacific convergence zone and the sea region west of 160°W, where it reaches a peak of 0.4 psu/(10 a)  [19,20] . To investigate the significant impact of corrosive medium concentration on weld joints, this study conducted electrochemical tests in the three zones using different NaCl solutions. The study found that the corrosion patterns of the base metal (BM) and fusion zone (FZ) were similar, whereas the heat-affected zone (HAZ) exhibited contrasting behavior. Specifically, for HSLA ship steel and ship steel welds, high-salinity seawater was more advantageous, while HAZ became the weakest link. However, in the actual service environment, the instability of the corrosion products increased further, which could easily lead to brittle cracking. Therefore, subsequent research will focus on optimizing the welding process, post-treatment of welded materials, and exploring effective methods to improve the material’s corrosion resistance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
(1) 
                            After undergoing optimized heat treatment, the HSLA ship steel exhibits a microstructure composed of pearlite and ferrite, which significantly improves its tensile and yield performance. The corrosion tests revealed that higher exposure concentrations correlate with better corrosion resistance, which can be attributed to the controlled mixture of hydrogen evolution and oxygen reduction. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Following the welding process, the interface exhibited a high level of uniformity and strong bonding. Simultaneously, the heat-affected zone displayed a microstructure consisting of pearlite, acicular ferrite, and grain boundary ferrite. The results of corrosion tests revealed a preferential corrosive morphology, indicating that higher concentrations of exposure were associated with lesser corrosion resistance due to the presence of multiple phases. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The corrosion tendency of the fusion zone in discrepancy NaCl concentration was found to be comparable to that of the base metal based on the results of corrosion tests. However, the presence of numerous microvoids and microcracks in the FZ suggested a decrease in corrosion resistance. This deterioration can be attributed to the coarsening of the microstructure and the presence of granular bainite.
